hand/quantum-field-theory.html:
Path Integral Quantization and Generating Functionals

The path integral formulation replaces canonical commutators with a sum over all field configurations weighted by eiS[φ]/ħ. For a real scalar field the transition amplitude between an initial configuration φi(x) at time ti and a final configuration φf(x) at tf is

⟨φf,tf|φi,ti⟩ = ∫𝒟φ exp[i∫d⁴x ℒ(φ,∂φ)] ,

where the functional measure 𝒟φ denotes integration over all fields that satisfy the boundary conditions. The generating functional Z[J] = ∫𝒟φ exp[i∫d⁴x(ℒ + Jφ)] encodes all correlation functions; functional differentiation with respect to the source J(x) yields time‑ordered Green’s functions:

⟨0|T{φ(x₁)…φ(xₙ)}|0⟩ = (−i)ⁿ δⁿZ[J]/δJ(x₁)…δJ(xₙ) |J=0 .

The connected generating functional W[J] = −i ln Z[J] produces connected diagrams, while the effective action Γ[φc] obtained by Legendre transformation of W[J] generates one‑particle‑irreducible (1PI) vertices. In perturbation theory the free part of the action is Gaussian, giving the propagator as the inverse of the kinetic operator, and interactions appear as vertices in the expansion of exp[i∫d⁴x ℒint]. The path integral makes manifest the role of symmetries: a change of integration variables corresponding to a symmetry leaves the measure invariant (up to possible Jacobians) and yields Ward–Takahashi identities for the Green’s functions. Gauge fixing is implemented by inserting a delta functional δ(G(A)−ω) and the associated Faddeev–Popov determinant, which can be exponentiated as a ghost action. This framework underlies modern proofs of renormalizability and the construction of non‑perturbative definitions such as lattice gauge theory.

Renormalization Group, Beta Functions and Asymptotic Freedom

The renormalization group (RG) describes how the effective couplings of a quantum field theory change with the energy scale μ at which the theory is probed. Starting from a bare Lagrangian defined at a cutoff Λ, one integrates out momentum shells between Λ and μ, generating a Wilsonian effective action Seff[φ;μ]. The flow of the dimensionless couplings gi(μ) is governed by the beta functions βi(g) = μ ∂gi/∂μ. In a mass‑independent scheme such as minimal subtraction (MS̅), the beta function can be computed as a series in the couplings. For a non‑Abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(N) and nf Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation, the one‑loop beta function is

β(g) = −(g³/16π²)[(11/3)N − (2/3)nf] .

When the coefficient is negative the coupling decreases at high momentum — asymptotic freedom — a hallmark of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) with N=3 and nf≤16. Conversely, quantum electrodynamics (QED) has a positive one‑loop coefficient β(e) = e³/12π², so the fine‑structure constant grows logarithmically with energy. The RG equation for the running coupling α(μ) = g²(μ)/4π integrates to

α(μ) = α(μ₀) / [1 − (β₀/2π) α(μ₀) ln(μ/μ₀)] ,

where β₀ is the first coefficient of the beta function. Higher‑loop corrections modify the running and introduce scheme dependence beyond two loops. Fixed points of the RG flow (β(g*)=0) correspond to scale‑invariant theories; the Gaussian fixed point g*=0 is ultraviolet (UV) stable for asymptotically free theories, while interacting fixed points (e.g. the Wilson–Fisher fixed point in three‑dimensional φ⁴ theory) control critical phenomena. The RG also dictates the scaling dimensions of operators: an operator 𝒪 with classical dimension d𝒪 acquires an anomalous dimension γ𝒪(g) so that its full dimension is Δ = d𝒪 + γ𝒪. This underpins the operator product expansion and the classification of relevant, marginal, and irrelevant operators in effective field theories.

Worked Example: One‑Loop Beta Function in QCD
Compute the one‑loop beta function coefficient β₀ for SU(3) gauge theory with nf = 5 active quark flavours. State whether the theory is asymptotically free.
For SU(N) with nf Dirac fermions, β₀ = (11/3)N − (2/3)nf. Substituting N = 3 and nf = 5 gives β₀ = (11/3)·3 − (2/3)·5 = 11 − 10/3 = 23/3 > 0. Since the beta function is β(g) = −β₀ g³/(16π²), a positive β₀ makes β(g) negative, so the coupling decreases at high momentum. Therefore QCD with five flavours is asymptotically free.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sign of the beta function, first write the general one‑loop formula, plug in the group‑theory factors (CA for gauge bosons, TF for fermions), and check the sign of the overall coefficient. Remember that asymptotic freedom ⇔ β₀ > 0 ⇔ negative β(g). A quick mental check: pure Yang–Mills (no fermions) always has β₀ = 11CA/3 > 0.

Anomalies, Ward Identities and the Axial Anomaly

A classical symmetry that fails to survive quantization is called an anomaly. In the path integral language an anomaly arises when the functional measure 𝒟ψ 𝒟ψ̄ is not invariant under a chiral transformation ψ → eiαγ⁵ψ. The Jacobian of this transformation produces a term proportional to the topological density Fμν F̃μν, leading to the celebrated Adler–Bell–Jackiw (ABJ) axial anomaly:

∂μJμ5 = (g²/16π²) Tr[Fμν F̃μν] ,

where Jμ5 = ψ̄γμγ⁵ψ is the axial current and F̃μν = ½εμνρσFρσ. The anomaly coefficient is fixed by the triangle diagram with one axial and two vector currents; it is proportional to the symmetric trace Tr[Ta{Tb,Tc}] over the fermion representation. In the Standard Model the gauge anomalies cancel because the sum of charges over each generation satisfies Σ QL = Σ QR for every gauge group factor, a non‑trivial constraint that dictates the hypercharge assignments of quarks and leptons. Ward identities, derived from the invariance of the generating functional under (non‑anomalous) symmetry transformations, relate Green’s functions with different numbers of external legs. For example, the QED Ward identity kμΓμ(p',p) = S⁻¹(p') − S⁻¹(p) guarantees that the photon remains massless to all orders in perturbation theory. When an anomaly is present, the Ward identity acquires an extra term equal to the anomaly, signalling the non‑conservation of the associated current. The axial anomaly explains the decay π⁰ → γγ and the η′ mass in QCD, and it underlies the topological interpretation of baryon number violation in electroweak theory (sphaleron processes).

Effective Field Theories and Power Counting

Effective field theory (EFT) provides a systematic framework for describing physics at energies E well below a heavy scale Λ. One writes the most general Lagrangian consistent with the low‑energy symmetries, organized as an expansion in operators of increasing mass dimension:

ℒEFT = ℒren + Σi (ci/Λdi−4) 𝒪i ,

where ℒren contains all renormalizable (dimension ≤4) operators, and the higher‑dimensional operators 𝒪i are suppressed by powers of E/Λ. Power counting assigns each operator a scaling dimension; at a given order in (E/Λ) only a finite number of operators contribute, making the theory predictive despite an infinite tower of terms. A classic example is the Fermi theory of weak interactions, where the four‑fermion operator (ψ̄γμ(1−γ⁵)ψ)² has dimension six and coefficient GF/√2 ∼ 1/Λ² with Λ ≈ 300 GeV. Loop diagrams in an EFT generate divergences that are absorbed by renormalizing the coefficients ci; the renormalization group then resums large logarithms ln(μ/Λ). Matching conditions at the scale Λ relate the EFT coefficients to the parameters of the underlying ultraviolet‑complete theory (e.g. the Standard Model). The chiral perturbation theory (χPT) for pions expands in momenta over the chiral symmetry breaking scale 4πfπ ≈ 1 GeV, while heavy‑quark effective theory (HQET) expands in 1/mQ. In all cases the EFT logic separates short‑distance physics (encoded in Wilson coefficients) from long‑distance dynamics (described by light fields), enabling precision calculations such as the determination of |Vcb| from B‑meson decays.

  • Confusing the sign convention of the beta function: β(g) = μ ∂g/∂μ versus β(g) = −β₀ g³/(16π²). Always state which definition you use.
  • Assuming all symmetries of the classical action survive quantization; remember that chiral gauge symmetries can be anomalous and must cancel in a consistent theory.
  • Treating the path integral measure as trivially invariant; the Fujikawa method shows the measure contributes the anomaly.
  • Neglecting operator mixing under renormalization in EFTs; higher‑dimensional operators can mix into lower‑dimensional ones, altering power counting.
  • Using the tree‑level propagator in loop integrals without the iε prescription; the prescription fixes the contour and ensures causality.
  • Forgetting that the Ward identity for a gauge symmetry guarantees the transversality of the gauge‑boson self‑energy, which protects the photon mass.
  • Misapplying the LSZ reduction formula by omitting the wave‑function renormalization factors Z½ for each external leg.

These advanced topics complete the bridge from textbook quantisation to the modern toolkit used in precision collider phenomenology and theoretical model building.

hand/mean-curvature-flow.html:
Type I and Type II Singularities and Blow‑up Analysis

In the study of mean curvature flow, singularities are classified by the rate at which the maximal curvature blows up as the singular time T is approached. A singularity is called Type I if the curvature satisfies max |A|² ≤ C/(T−t) for some constant C; equivalently, the rescaled flow Mₜ = λ(t)(Mₜ − x₀) with λ(t) = (T−t)⁻¹ᐟ² has uniformly bounded curvature. Type I singularities are the most common and include the shrinking sphere, the shrinking cylinder Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ, and the translating bowl soliton after appropriate parabolic rescaling. Huisken’s monotonicity formula guarantees that any Type I blow‑up limit is a self‑shrinker satisfying H = (x·ν)/2.

Type II singularities occur when the curvature blows up faster than (T−t)⁻¹ᐟ². In this case one must choose a sequence of space‑time points where the curvature achieves a suitable maximum and rescale by the curvature itself. The resulting limits are ancient solutions (defined for all negative times) that are not self‑shrinkers. Famous examples include the Angenent torus in ℝ³ and the translating solitons (bowl soliton, grim reaper curve). The distinction is crucial for surgery constructions: Huisken–Sinestrari proved that two‑convex flows only develop Type I singularities, which makes the surgery procedure possible. For general mean‑convex flows, Type II singularities can appear, and their analysis requires the machinery of blow‑up sequences and entropy introduced by Colding–Minicozzi.

Blow‑up analysis proceeds by selecting a sequence (xₖ, tₖ) with tₖ → T and |A|(xₖ, tₖ) = maxMₜₖ |A|. One then defines the rescaled flows Mₖ(s) = λₖ (Mtₖ + s/λₖ² − xₖ) with λₖ = |A|(xₖ, tₖ). By the compactness theorem for Brakke flows (or the level‑set compactness), a subsequence converges to a limit flow defined for all s ∈ (−∞, 0] (Type I) or s ∈ (−∞, ∞) (Type II). The limit is a smooth ancient solution of MCF. Classifying these limits is a central problem: in ℝ³, the only compact ancient solutions are the shrinking sphere and the Angenent torus; non‑compact ones include the shrinking cylinder, the translating bowl, and the ancient ovals constructed by Angenent–Daskalopoulos–Sesum.

Examiners often test the ability to distinguish Type I from Type II by giving a curvature bound and asking which classification applies. A typical trap is to assume that any blow‑up limit of a mean‑convex flow must be a cylinder; however, the translating bowl soliton is a Type II limit that can arise from a mean‑convex initial surface. Another common error is to confuse the parabolic rescaling factor λ(t) = (T−t)⁻¹ᐟ² with the curvature‑dependent rescaling used for Type II analysis.

Ancient Solutions and Self‑Shrinkers in Mean Curvature Flow

An ancient solution of MCF is a smooth family of hypersurfaces {Mₜ}ₜ<₀ defined for all negative times. Self‑shrinkers are a special class of ancient solutions that evolve by homothety: Mₜ = √(−t) M₋₁. They satisfy the elliptic equation H = (x·ν)/2 and correspond to critical points of the Gaussian area functional F(M) = (4π)⁻ⁿᐟ² ∫_M e−|x|²/4 dμ. Huisken’s monotonicity formula shows that the Gaussian density at a singular point equals the F‑value of any blow‑up limit, which must be a self‑shrinker.

The classification of self‑shrinkers is far from complete in high dimensions, but in ℝ³ significant progress has been made. Brendle (2016) proved that the only embedded self‑shrinkers of genus zero are the sphere, the cylinder, and the plane. For higher genus, the Angenent torus provides a non‑trivial example. Colding–Minicozzi (2012) introduced the entropy of a hypersurface, λ(M) = supx₀,t₀>0 Fx₀,t₀(M), where Fx₀,t₀ is the Gaussian area centered at x₀ with scale t₀. They showed that entropy is non‑increasing along MCF and that low‑entropy self‑shrinkers are rigid: any self‑shrinker with entropy less than that of the cylinder must be a plane or a sphere.

Ancient solutions that are not self‑shrinkers include translating solitons (solutions moving by a constant velocity vector v with H = v·ν) and the ancient ovals (compact, convex, non‑collapsed ancient solutions that are not self‑similar). The classification of convex ancient solutions in ℝⁿ⁺¹ was completed by Choi–Haslhofer–Hershkovits (2019) and independently by Brendle–Choi (2019): the only compact convex ancient solutions are the shrinking spheres; the only non‑compact ones are the shrinking cylinders Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ, the translating bowl soliton, and the ancient ovals (which exist only for n=1, i.e., curves). This classification is a cornerstone for the mean‑convex neighborhood conjecture and for the surgery program in higher dimensions.

In examinations, a typical question asks to identify the possible blow‑up limits at a singularity of a two‑convex flow. The correct answer uses the fact that two‑convexity forces Type I singularities, so every blow‑up limit is a self‑shrinker with non‑negative mean curvature. By the Huisken–Sinestrari theorem, the only such self‑shrinkers are the sphere and the cylinder. A frequent mistake is to list the translating bowl soliton as a possible limit; it has zero mean curvature at its tip and is not a self‑shrinker, hence cannot appear as a Type I blow‑up.

Worked Example: Classifying a Singularity
Consider a smooth, closed, two‑convex hypersurface M₀ ⊂ ℝ⁴ evolving by MCF. Suppose the flow develops a singularity at time T and at a point x₀. The Gaussian density at (x₀,T) is computed to be Θ = 1.5. Determine all possible tangent flows at this singularity.
Step 1: Two‑convexity implies the singularity is Type I (Huisken–Sinestrari). Therefore every tangent flow is a self‑shrinker. Step 2: The Gaussian density of a self‑shrinker equals its F‑value. Known values: plane F=1, sphere F≈1.57 (for S³), cylinder S²×ℝ has F≈1.57 as well? Actually F(S²×ℝ) = F(S²) ≈ 1.57. The given density 1.5 is less than the sphere/cylinder value but greater than the plane. However, by Colding–Minicozzi, any self‑shrinker with entropy λ < λ(S²×ℝ) must be a plane. Since the Gaussian density at a singular point equals the entropy of the tangent flow, and 1.5 < λ(S²×ℝ), the only possibility is a plane. But a plane has density 1, contradiction. Therefore the assumed density 1.5 cannot occur for a two‑convex flow in ℝ⁴. The correct conclusion: the only possible tangent flows are the shrinking sphere S³ and the shrinking cylinder S²×ℝ, both with density ≈1.57. Hence the given density is inconsistent with two‑convexity; the problem tests recognition that two‑convex singularities have densities at least that of the cylinder.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for possible blow‑up limits, first decide whether the flow is two‑convex or merely mean‑convex. Two‑convex ⇒ Type I ⇒ limits are self‑shrinkers with λ₁+λ₂≥0. Mean‑convex ⇒ Type II may appear ⇒ translating solitons and ancient ovals are also admissible. Memorise the Gaussian densities of the basic self‑shrinkers (plane=1, cylinder≈1.57, sphere≈1.57 in ℝ⁴) and the entropy bound λ(cylinder). This allows quick elimination of impossible limits.

Mean Curvature Flow with Boundary Conditions and Free Boundary Problems

Mean curvature flow with boundary arises when the evolving hypersurface meets a fixed supporting hypersurface ∂Ω in the ambient manifold. Two standard boundary conditions are the Dirichlet condition (the boundary of the flowing surface is fixed on ∂Ω) and the Neumann (free boundary) condition (the surface meets ∂Ω orthogonally, i.e., the conormal is tangent to ∂Ω). The free boundary problem is particularly natural for capillary surfaces and for the study of minimal surfaces with free boundary.

Short‑time existence for smooth initial data with either boundary condition follows from the same parabolic theory as the closed case, using the DeTurck trick or the Nash–Moser implicit function theorem. For the free boundary problem, the orthogonal intersection condition is preserved by the flow because the evolution equation for the contact angle is a homogeneous linear parabolic equation. Stahl (1996) proved that if the initial hypersurface is convex and meets the boundary of a convex domain orthogonally, the flow exists until it shrinks to a point on the boundary, and the rescaled limit is a hemisphere.

Singularity analysis for free boundary MCF parallels the closed case. Huisken’s monotonicity formula adapts by reflecting the flow across the boundary, yielding a monotone quantity for the doubled flow. Consequently, Type I singularities are modeled on self‑shrinkers with free boundary (half‑spheres, half‑cylinders). The classification of free‑boundary self‑shrinkers in a half‑space was completed by Edelen (2020): the only smooth, properly embedded ones are the half‑plane, the half‑sphere, and the half‑cylinder Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ meeting the boundary orthogonally.

Applications include the proof of the free‑boundary isoperimetric inequality in convex domains via MCF, and the construction of minimal surfaces with free boundary by flowing to a minimal limit. In examinations, a typical question asks whether the orthogonal contact angle is preserved under MCF with Neumann condition. The answer is yes, because the evolution of the angle satisfies a linear parabolic PDE with zero initial data, so the maximum principle forces it to remain zero. A common trap is to assume that the Dirichlet condition (fixed boundary) also preserves convexity; it does not in general, and the flow may develop interior singularities even if the initial surface is convex.

Higher Codimension Mean Curvature Flow and the Andrews‑Baker Pinching Theorem

When the evolving submanifold has codimension greater than one, the mean curvature vector H is normal to the submanifold, and the flow equation is ∂ₜ x = H. The geometry is richer: the second fundamental form is a vector‑valued tensor, and curvature pinching conditions involve the eigenvalues of the second fundamental form in each normal direction. A fundamental result is the Andrews‑Baker theorem (2010): if a compact submanifold Mⁿ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺ᵏ satisfies the pinching condition |A|² < (2/(n+2)) |H|² (or the stronger condition |A|² ≤ (1/n) |H|² for n≥2), then this condition is preserved by MCF and the flow converges to a round point after rescaling. This generalises Huisken’s convexity pinching for hypersurfaces (where |A|² ≤ (1/n) H² is equivalent to convexity).

The proof uses the evolution equations for |A|² and |H|² and a maximum principle argument for a suitably chosen quantity Q = |A|² − c|H|². The optimal constant c = 2/(n+2) is sharp; examples of submanifolds violating the condition can develop Type II singularities or converge to non‑spherical self‑shrinkers such as the Clifford torus Sᵐ(√m) × Sⁿ⁻ᵐ(√(n−m)) in the sphere, which under stereographic projection gives a self‑shrinker in Euclidean space.

Another important development is the mean curvature flow of Lagrangian submanifolds in Kähler–Einstein manifolds. Smoczyk (1996) showed that the Lagrangian condition is preserved, and the flow can be expressed as a gradient flow of the volume functional. In ℂⁿ, the only compact Lagrangian self‑shrinkers are the Clifford torus and its rotations (proved by Neves, 2007). This connects MCF to the Hamiltonian stationary condition and to mirror symmetry.

Examiners often test the distinction between hypersurface and higher‑codimension pinching. A typical multiple‑choice question gives the inequality |A|² ≤ (1/n) |H|² and asks whether it is preserved for codimension >1. The answer is no; the correct preserved condition is |A|² ≤ (2/(n+2)) |H|². Another trap is to confuse the Andrews‑Baker pinching with the Hamilton‑Ivey pinching for Ricci flow; they are analogous but belong to different geometric flows.

Entropy, Generic Singularities, and the Colding‑Minicozzi Uniqueness Theorem

The concept of entropy introduced by Colding and Minicozzi (2012) provides a quantitative measure of the complexity of a singularity. For a hypersurface M, the entropy is λ(M) = supx₀∈ℝⁿ⁺¹, t₀>0 (4π t₀)⁻ⁿᐟ² ∫_M e−|x−x₀|²/(4t₀) dμ. Entropy is non‑increasing along MCF and is additive under disjoint union. The entropy of a self‑shrinker equals its Gaussian density. Colding–Minicozzi proved that if a singularity has entropy strictly less than that of the cylinder Sⁿ⁻¹ × ℝ, then the singularity is generic in the sense that the tangent flow is unique and is a multiplicity‑one sphere or plane. Moreover, they showed that the set of initial data producing non‑generic singularities (entropy ≥ λ(cylinder)) is of infinite codimension in the space of smooth embeddings, justifying the term “generic”.

The uniqueness theorem states that for a generic singularity, any sequence of parabolic rescalings converges to the same tangent flow (a round sphere). This resolves a long‑standing question about the uniqueness of blow‑up limits. The proof uses the Łojasiewicz‑Simon gradient inequality for the Gaussian area functional near a non‑degenerate critical point (the sphere). The non‑degeneracy follows from the spectral analysis of the Ornstein‑Uhlenbeck operator on the sphere, where the first non‑zero eigenvalue is 1/2.

These results have profound implications for the mean‑convex neighborhood conjecture and for the construction of MCF with surgery in higher dimensions. In particular, they imply that for a generic mean‑convex initial hypersurface, all singularities are spherical or cylindrical, and the surgery procedure of Huisken–Sinestrari can be carried out without encountering exotic Type II singularities. The entropy also provides a monotone quantity that can be used to define a weak flow through singularities by selecting the branch with minimal entropy, an alternative to Brakke’s varifold approach.

In examinations, a common question asks to compute the entropy of the cylinder Sⁿ⁻¹ × ℝ and compare it with the entropy of the sphere. The entropy of the cylinder is λ(Sⁿ⁻¹) = (4π)⁻⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾ᐟ² ∫Sⁿ⁻¹ e−|x|²/4 dμ, which is strictly larger than the entropy of the sphere Sⁿ. Students must remember that the cylinder has higher entropy because it is non‑compact and its Gaussian integral factorises. A frequent error is to claim that the sphere has higher entropy because it is “more curved”.

  • Confusing Type I and Type II rescaling factors: Type I uses (T−t)⁻¹ᐟ², Type II uses the curvature itself.
  • Assuming every blow‑up limit of a mean‑convex flow is a cylinder; translating solitons and ancient ovals are also possible.
  • Stating that the orthogonal contact angle is not preserved under free‑boundary MCF; it is preserved by the maximum principle.
  • Applying the hypersurface pinching condition |A|² ≤ (1/n) H² to higher codimension; the correct constant is 2/(n+2).
  • Believing the sphere has higher entropy than the cylinder; the cylinder’s entropy is larger because of its non‑compact factor.
  • Thinking that generic singularities can have non‑unique tangent flows; Colding‑Minicozzi proved uniqueness for entropy below the cylinder threshold.
  • Overlooking that two‑convexity forces Type I singularities only; Type II singularities cannot occur in the two‑convex class.
The advanced topics above complete the theoretical toolkit needed to analyse singularities, boundary behaviour, higher codimension, and generic properties of mean curvature flow.

hand/info-theory.html:
Network Information Theory — Multiple Access and Broadcast Channels

Classical point‑to‑point channel coding extends naturally to multi‑user settings where several transmitters share a common medium or a single transmitter serves many receivers. The multiple‑access channel (MAC) models K independent senders X₁,…,X_K communicating to a single receiver Y. The capacity region is the set of rate tuples (R₁,…,R_K) satisfying, for every subset S ⊆ {1,…,K},

Σi∈S R_i ≤ I(X_S ; Y | XS^c)

where the mutual informations are evaluated under a product input distribution p(x₁)…p(x_K). This region, proved by Ahlswede (1971) and Liao (1972), is a polymatroid; its corner points are achieved by successive decoding (SIC) where the receiver decodes users one by one while treating the rest as noise. The Slepian‑Wolf theorem (1973) gives the dual source‑coding result: correlated sources can be compressed separately at rates approaching the joint entropy, provided the sum rate exceeds H(X₁,…,X_K).

The broadcast channel (BC) reverses the topology: one sender X transmits to K receivers Y₁,…,Y_K. The capacity region is known only for special cases. For the degraded BC (where Y₁ → Y₂ → … → Y_K forms a Markov chain), Cover (1972) showed that superposition coding achieves the region R₁ ≤ I(U;Y₁), R₂ ≤ I(X;Y₂|U) for some auxiliary U → X → (Y₁,Y₂). Marton’s inner bound (1979) uses two independent auxiliaries U₁,U₂ and a common message W to enlarge the region for general BCs. The best known outer bound remains the UVW bound (Nair‑El Gamal, 2009). For the Gaussian BC with power constraint P and noise variances N₁ ≤ N₂, the capacity region is exactly the set of (R₁,R₂) with R₁ ≤ ½ log₂(1+αP/N₁), R₂ ≤ ½ log₂(1+(1−α)P/(αP+N₂)) for some α∈[0,1].

These multi‑user results underpin modern wireless standards: NOMA (non‑orthogonal multiple access) in 5G implements SIC on the uplink MAC, while downlink MU‑MIMO uses dirty‑paper coding (Costa, 1983) — a BC technique that pre‑cancels known interference — to achieve the sum capacity of the Gaussian MIMO BC. Understanding the geometry of polymatroids and the role of auxiliary random variables is essential for any advanced treatment of network information theory.

Information Geometry and the Fisher Information Metric

Information geometry treats a family of probability distributions {p_θ} as a differentiable manifold whose points are parameter vectors θ∈Θ⊆ℝ^d. The Fisher information matrix I(θ) with entries Iij(θ)=E_θ[∂_i log p_θ(X) ∂_j log p_θ(X)] defines a Riemannian metric on this manifold. For an exponential family p_θ(x)=h(x)exp(θ·T(x)−A(θ)), the metric simplifies to the Hessian of the log‑partition function: I(θ)=∇²A(θ). This makes the manifold dually flat: the natural parameters θ and the expectation parameters η=∇A(θ) are connected by a Legendre transform, and the Kullback‑Leibler divergence D_KL(p_θ‖pθ') acts as a Bregman divergence generated by A.

The α‑connections introduced by Amari (1985) interpolate between the exponential (α=1) and mixture (α=−1) affine structures. The Levi‑Civita connection of the Fisher metric corresponds to α=0. Geodesics under the exponential connection are straight lines in θ‑space; under the mixture connection they are straight lines in η‑space. This duality yields the Pythagorean theorem for KL divergence: if a submanifold is e‑flat and another is m‑flat and they intersect orthogonally, then D_KL(p‖r)=D_KL(p‖q)+D_KL(q‖r) for the projection points. The Cramér‑Rao bound follows directly: for any unbiased estimator θ̂, Cov(θ̂) ≥ I(θ)−1, with equality iff the estimator is efficient and the model is an exponential family.

Applications abound. In variational inference, the natural gradient ∇̃L = I(θ)−1∇L follows the steepest descent direction on the statistical manifold, often accelerating convergence dramatically. In neural network training, the Fisher matrix approximates the curvature of the loss landscape, motivating methods such as K‑FAC (Kronecker‑factored Approximate Curvature). In quantum information, the quantum Fisher information metric governs the ultimate precision of parameter estimation (the quantum Cramér‑Rao bound). Mastery of these geometric concepts provides a unified language linking estimation theory, optimization, and the structure of statistical models.

Worked Example: MAC Sum‑Rate with Binary Inputs
Two users transmit independent Bernoulli(½) bits over a binary adder MAC: Y = X₁ ⊕ X₂ ⊕ Z, where Z∼Bernoulli(p) is independent noise. Compute the maximum achievable sum rate R₁+R₂.
For the binary adder MAC the output Y is the modulo‑2 sum of the three independent bits. Since X₁ and X₂ are uniform, X₁⊕X₂ is also uniform and independent of Z. Hence Y is Bernoulli(½) regardless of p, so H(Y)=1 bit. The conditional entropy H(Y|X₁,X₂)=H(Z)=h₂(p) where h₂ is the binary entropy function. The sum‑rate bound from the MAC region is R₁+R₂ ≤ I(X₁,X₂;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y|X₁,X₂)=1−h₂(p). This bound is tight because independent uniform inputs achieve the corner point of the polymatroid. Therefore the maximum sum rate is 1−h₂(p) bits per channel use.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a multi‑user region is asked, first identify whether the problem describes a MAC or a BC. Write the generic single‑letter bounds (MAC: subset inequalities; BC: degraded or Marton inner bound). Then check for special structure — degradedness, Gaussian noise, binary symmetry — that collapses the region to a simple parametric form. Sketch the polymatroid or the BC region; visualising corner points often reveals the optimal time‑sharing or power‑splitting parameter without heavy algebra.

Secrecy Capacity and the Wiretap Channel

Wyner’s wiretap model (1975) adds an eavesdropper Z to the point‑to‑point channel X→Y. The sender wishes to transmit a message W to the legitimate receiver while keeping I(W;Z^n) arbitrarily small. The secrecy capacity is C_s = maxp(x) [I(X;Y) − I(X;Z)]⁺, where [·]⁺ denotes the positive part. The achievability uses stochastic encoding: the message selects a bin, and the codeword is chosen uniformly from that bin; the binning rate equals I(X;Z) so that the eavesdropper’s observation is nearly independent of the message. The converse follows from Fano’s inequality and the data‑processing inequality applied to the Markov chain W → X^n → (Y^n,Z^n).

Csiszár and Körner (1978) generalized this to the broadcast channel with confidential messages: a common message W₀ for both receivers and a private message W₁ for receiver 1 that must be kept secret from receiver 2. The capacity region consists of rate pairs (R₀,R₁) satisfying R₀ ≤ min{I(U;Y₁), I(U;Y₂)}, R₁ ≤ I(V;Y₁|U) − I(V;Y₂|U) for some U → V → X → (Y₁,Y₂). The auxiliary U carries the common information, while V carries the confidential part; the difference of mutual informations is the secrecy penalty. For the Gaussian wiretap channel with signal‑to‑noise ratios SNR_B (Bob) and SNR_E (Eve), the secrecy capacity simplifies to ½ log₂( (1+SNR_B)/(1+SNR_E) ) when SNR_B > SNR_E, and zero otherwise.

Modern extensions include secret‑key agreement from correlated sources (Maurer, 1993), where two parties observing X^n and Y^n can generate a shared secret key at rate I(X;Y) − I(X;Z) if an eavesdropper sees Z^n. In physical‑layer security, artificial noise and beamforming exploit multiple antennas to enlarge the legitimate channel’s advantage. The information‑theoretic secrecy framework remains the gold standard because it guarantees security against computationally unbounded adversaries, unlike computational cryptography.

Feedback Capacity and the Role of Feedback in Channel Coding

Shannon proved in 1956 that for a discrete memoryless channel (DMC) the capacity with noiseless feedback CFB equals the ordinary capacity C. The proof uses the fact that feedback cannot increase the maximum of I(X;Y) over input distributions because the channel law p(y|x) remains unchanged and the directed information I(X^n→Y^n) reduces to Σ I(X_i;Y_i|Yi-1) ≤ Σ I(X_i;Y_i) ≤ nC. However, feedback can dramatically simplify coding schemes and improve error exponents. The Schalkwijk‑Kailath scheme (1966) for the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel with feedback achieves the capacity C = ½ log₂(1+P/N) with a linear encoder that transmits the estimation error; the error probability decays doubly exponentially in blocklength.

For channels with memory, feedback can strictly increase capacity. The classic example is the trapdoor channel (Cover & Pombra, 1989) where the state depends on past inputs; feedback lets the transmitter learn the state and adapt. In the Gaussian channel with intersymbol interference (ISI), the feedback capacity is given by the water‑filling solution over the power spectral density of the noise, which can be larger than the non‑feedback capacity when the noise spectrum is non‑flat. The directed information I(X^n→Y^n) = Σ I(X_i;Y_i|Yi-1) is the correct information measure for feedback channels, and the capacity is CFB = limn→∞ (1/n) maxp(x^n||yn-1) I(X^n→Y^n), where the maximisation is over causally conditioned input distributions.

Practical systems exploit feedback through hybrid ARQ (HARQ) and adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) in LTE/5G. Although these do not increase the Shannon capacity of the underlying memoryless fading channel, they achieve rates close to the ergodic capacity with far lower latency and complexity than non‑feedback codes. Understanding when feedback helps — and when it does not — is a recurring theme in both theoretical exams and system design.

Zero‑Error Capacity and Graph Entropy

Shannon’s zero‑error capacity C₀ of a channel asks for the maximum rate at which messages can be transmitted with exactly zero probability of error, not merely asymptotically vanishing error. For a DMC with input alphabet 𝒳 and output alphabet 𝒴, define the confusability graph G on 𝒳: two distinct inputs x,x' are adjacent if there exists an output y with p(y|x)>0 and p(y|x')>0. A set of inputs is an independent set in G iff no two are confusable; thus a zero‑error code of length n corresponds to an independent set in the strong graph product G⊠n. The zero‑error capacity is C₀ = limn→∞ (1/n) log₂ α(G⊠n), where α(·) denotes the independence number.

Lovász (1979) introduced the theta function ϑ(G), a semidefinite‑programming relaxation of α(G), and proved α(G) ≤ ϑ(G) ≤ χ(G) (the clique cover number of the complement). Moreover, ϑ(G⊠n) = ϑ(G)^n, so C₀ ≤ log₂ ϑ(G). For the pentagon graph C₅, α(C₅)=2 but ϑ(C₅)=√5, giving C₀ = ½ log₂ 5 ≈ 1.16 bits, strictly larger than log₂ α(C₅)=1. This was the first demonstration that C₀ can exceed the single‑letter independence number.

Graph entropy H_G(P), defined by Körner (1973) for a probability distribution P on the vertices, measures the minimum rate of a random coloring that separates adjacent vertices with high probability. It satisfies H_G(P) ≤ H(P) and appears in the source‑coding problem with side information (the Körner‑Marton problem). The zero‑error capacity of a channel with state known at the transmitter is given by the maximum of H_G(P) over input distributions. These combinatorial quantities connect information theory to extremal graph theory, semidefinite programming, and quantum non‑locality (the Lovász theta function equals the maximum quantum value of a certain Bell inequality).

  • Confusing the MAC sum‑rate bound with the individual user bounds; remember the polymatroid structure requires all subset inequalities.
  • Assuming feedback always increases capacity; it does not for memoryless channels but can for channels with memory.
  • Treating the wiretap secrecy capacity as I(X;Y)−I(X;Z) without the positive part; if the eavesdropper’s channel is better, the secrecy capacity is zero.
  • Mixing up the Lovász theta function with the Shannon capacity of a graph; ϑ(G) upper‑bounds the zero‑error capacity, not the ordinary Shannon capacity.
  • Neglecting the auxiliary random variables in broadcast‑channel inner bounds; superposition coding and Marton’s scheme both rely on carefully chosen U,V.
  • Applying the Cramér‑Rao bound to biased estimators without the bias‑correction term; the bound holds only for unbiased estimators or with the appropriate mean‑square‑error matrix.
  • Overlooking the dual flatness of exponential families in information geometry; the natural and expectation parameters are linked by a Legendre transform, not a simple linear map.

These advanced topics complete the bridge from single‑user Shannon theory to modern network, security, and geometric perspectives that appear in graduate‑level examinations and research.

hand/electrochemistry.html:
Electrochemical Series and Predicting Redox Feasibility

The electrochemical series arranges half‑reactions in order of their standard reduction potentials (E°). A species with a more positive E° is a stronger oxidising agent, while a species with a more negative E° is a stronger reducing agent. To decide whether a redox reaction will proceed spontaneously under standard conditions, write the two half‑reactions as reductions, identify the cathode (the half‑reaction with the higher E°) and the anode (the lower E°), then calculate E°cell = E°cathode – E°anode. If E°cell > 0, the reaction is thermodynamically favourable; if E°cell < 0, an external voltage at least equal to |E°cell| is required. The series also allows rapid prediction of displacement reactions: a metal higher in the series (more negative E°) can reduce the cation of any metal lower in the series. For example, Zn (E° = –0.76 V) displaces Cu²⁺ (E° = +0.34 V) because the cell potential is +1.10 V. Conversely, Cu cannot displace Zn²⁺. The series is temperature‑dependent; at 298 K the values quoted in standard tables are used, but at other temperatures the Nernst equation must be applied to each half‑reaction before comparing. In practice, kinetic barriers (high overpotential) may prevent a thermodynamically allowed reaction from occurring at an observable rate, a point examiners often test by asking why a reaction with a positive E°cell does not proceed without a catalyst.

Liquid Junction Potentials and Salt Bridge Design

When two electrolyte solutions of different composition or concentration meet, a diffusion potential — the liquid junction potential (LJP) — arises because ions migrate at different speeds. In a galvanic cell the salt bridge (commonly KCl or KNO₃ in agar) minimises this potential by providing ions of nearly equal mobility (K⁺ and Cl⁻ have similar limiting molar conductivities, λ°K⁺ ≈ 73.5 S cm² mol⁻¹, λ°Cl⁻ ≈ 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹). The residual LJP for a KCl bridge is typically < 1 mV, whereas a bridge containing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ can give several millivolts because λ°Na⁺ ≈ 50.1 S cm² mol⁻¹. The Henderson equation quantifies the LJP: E_LJP = (RT/F) Σ (t_i – t_j) ln(a_i/a_j), where t_i are transference numbers. In high‑precision potentiometry (e.g., pH glass electrode calibration) the LJP is either measured and subtracted or eliminated by using a double‑junction reference electrode with an inner filling solution matching the test solution’s major ion. Examiners may ask to calculate the LJP for a junction between 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaCl, expecting the student to recognise that H⁺ mobility (λ°H⁺ ≈ 349.8 S cm² mol⁻¹) dominates, producing a junction potential of about +15 mV (HCl side positive). Proper salt‑bridge selection and temperature control are therefore essential for reproducible cell EMF measurements.

Worked Example: Estimating Liquid Junction Potential
A cell uses a salt bridge of 1 M KCl to connect a 0.01 M HCl half‑cell (anode) with a 0.01 M NaCl half‑cell (cathode). Assuming limiting ionic conductivities λ°H⁺ = 349.8, λ°K⁺ = 73.5, λ°Na⁺ = 50.1, λ°Cl⁻ = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹, estimate the liquid junction potential at 298 K.
For a KCl bridge the dominant ions are K⁺ and Cl⁻ with nearly equal mobilities, so the bridge contributes negligible LJP. The junction of interest is between the HCl solution (H⁺, Cl⁻) and the bridge (K⁺, Cl⁻). Using the Henderson approximation for a binary junction: E_LJP ≈ (RT/F) (t_H⁺ – t_K⁺) ln(a_H⁺/a_K⁺). Transference numbers t_i = λ_i / Σλ. In the HCl side Σλ ≈ λ_H⁺ + λ_Cl⁻ = 426.1; t_H⁺ ≈ 0.821. In the bridge Σλ ≈ λ_K⁺ + λ_Cl⁻ = 149.8; t_K⁺ ≈ 0.491. Thus t_H⁺ – t_K⁺ ≈ 0.330. Activities a_H⁺ ≈ 0.01, a_K⁺ ≈ 1 (bridge). ln(0.01/1) = –4.605. RT/F = 0.025693 V. E_LJP ≈ 0.025693 × 0.330 × (–4.605) ≈ –0.039 V = –39 mV. The negative sign means the HCl side is negative relative to the bridge. In practice the measured LJP is smaller because activity coefficients and finite concentrations reduce the effective mobility difference; a typical experimental value is –15 to –20 mV.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sign of a liquid junction potential, first identify which ion has the higher mobility in each solution. The side supplying the faster ion becomes positively charged. Memorise the order of limiting molar conductivities for common ions (H⁺ ≫ OH⁻ > K⁺ ≈ Cl⁻ > Na⁺ > Li⁺). This allows rapid qualitative answers without full Henderson calculations.

Electrode Kinetics: Butler‑Volmer Equation and Overpotential

Thermodynamics (Nernst equation) tells whether a reaction can occur; kinetics tells how fast. The Butler‑Volmer equation describes the current density (j) at an electrode as a function of overpotential (η = E – E_eq): j = j₀ [exp(α_a nF η / RT) – exp(–α_c nF η / RT)], where j₀ is the exchange current density, α_a and α_c are the anodic and cathodic transfer coefficients (α_a + α_c = 1 for a single‑step electron transfer), n is the number of electrons, and η is positive for anodic polarisation. At low overpotentials (|η| < ~10 mV) the equation linearises to j ≈ j₀ nF η / RT, defining the charge‑transfer resistance R_ct = RT / (j₀ nF). Large exchange current densities (e.g., Pt/H₂, j₀ ≈ 10⁻³ A cm⁻²) give small kinetic barriers; sluggish reactions such as O₂ evolution on Pt (j₀ ≈ 10⁻⁹ A cm⁻²) require substantial overpotentials (> 300 mV) to reach practical current densities. The Tafel equation, η = a + b log|j|, follows from the high‑overpotential limit of Butler‑Volmer: for anodic η > 0, η ≈ (RT/α_a nF) ln(j/j₀); for cathodic η < 0, η ≈ –(RT/α_c nF) ln(|j|/j₀). The Tafel slope b = 2.303 RT / (α nF) is a diagnostic tool: a slope of ~120 mV/decade at 298 K implies α ≈ 0.5 for a one‑electron step. Examiners frequently ask to extract α or j₀ from a Tafel plot, or to explain why hydrogen evolution on mercury shows a higher overpotential than on platinum (lower j₀ due to weaker H adsorption). Understanding the distinction between activation overpotential (charge‑transfer), concentration overpotential (mass‑transport), and ohmic drop (solution resistance) is essential for interpreting polarisation curves in corrosion and electrolysis problems.

Applications of Nernst Equation: pH Measurement and Ion‑Selective Electrodes

The glass electrode is the classic example of a Nernstian sensor. Its potential follows E = E°′ – (2.303 RT/F) pH, where E°′ includes the reference electrode potential and the asymmetry potential of the glass membrane. At 298 K the slope is –59.16 mV per pH unit. The membrane consists of a hydrated silica gel layer that exchanges H⁺ with the solution; the potential develops across this layer according to the Nernst equation for the half‑reaction H⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ ½ H₂ (formal). Ion‑selective electrodes (ISEs) for other ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, F⁻) operate on the same principle: a membrane selective to the target ion creates a phase‑boundary potential E = E°′ + (2.303 RT/zF) log a_i, where z is the ion charge. The Nikolsky‑Eisenman equation extends this to interfering ions: E = E°′ + (2.303 RT/z_i F) log (a_i + Σ K_ij a_jz_i/z_j). Selectivity coefficients K_ij are determined experimentally; a good ISE has K_ij < 10⁻³ for common interferents. Calibration curves are plotted as E versus log a_i; linearity over several decades confirms Nernstian behaviour. Temperature affects the slope (∂E/∂T = –(2.303 R/zF) log a_i), so modern meters incorporate automatic temperature compensation. In examinations, a typical question provides a set of measured potentials for standard buffers at two temperatures and asks to calculate the true pH of an unknown sample, requiring the student to apply the temperature‑corrected Nernst slope and to correct for the liquid junction potential of the reference electrode.

Industrial Electrolysis: Chlor‑alkali Process and Aluminium Production

The chlor‑alkali industry produces chlorine, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide by electrolysing brine (NaCl solution). Three cell technologies exist: mercury, diaphragm, and membrane. The membrane cell, now dominant, uses a cation‑exchange membrane (e.g., Nafion) that allows Na⁺ to pass but blocks Cl⁻ and OH⁻, yielding high‑purity NaOH (≈ 32 % w/w) and Cl₂ gas at the anode. The overall reaction is 2 NaCl + 2 H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2 NaOH. The theoretical cell voltage at 298 K is 2.19 V (E°cell = –2.19 V for the non‑spontaneous direction), but commercial cells operate at 3.0–3.5 V due to overpotentials (Cl₂ evolution ≈ 0.1 V, O₂ evolution on the cathode ≈ 0.3 V) and ohmic losses across the membrane. Energy consumption is ~ 2.5 MWh per tonne of Cl₂. Aluminium is produced by the Hall‑Héroult process: electrolysis of Al₂O₃ dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) at 950–970 °C. The cathode reaction is Al³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Al(l) (E° = –1.66 V vs SHE), the anode reaction is 2 O²⁻ → O₂ + 4 e⁻ (E° = +1.23 V), giving a reversible voltage of ~ 2.9 V. Practical cells run at 4.2–4.5 V because of the high overpotential for oxygen evolution on carbon anodes and the voltage drop across the electrolyte. Current efficiencies of 90–95 % are typical; the remainder is lost to side reactions (e.g., formation of CF₄). Faraday’s law gives the theoretical aluminium mass: m = (I t M) / (z F) = (I t × 26.98) / (3 × 96485) ≈ 9.33 × 10⁻⁵ I t (kg per ampere‑hour). A 300 kA cell thus produces ~ 28 kg Al per hour. Examiners often ask to compute the specific energy consumption (kWh/kg Al) from given current, voltage, and current efficiency, testing the ability to combine Faraday’s law with electrical power (P = V I).

  • Confusing the sign convention for overpotential: η = E_applied – E_eq; a positive η drives anodic current, negative η drives cathodic current.
  • Assuming the Nernst slope is always 0.059 V per decade; it is 0.05916 V/n at 298 K and varies with temperature.
  • Neglecting liquid junction potentials when comparing measured cell EMF with calculated standard potentials.
  • Using the wrong transfer coefficient (α) in the Tafel equation; α_a + α_c = 1 only for a single‑electron elementary step.
  • Treating the exchange current density j₀ as a constant for all electrode materials; it varies by orders of magnitude.
  • Forgetting that the membrane in a chlor‑alkali cell conducts only cations, so the anode and cathode compartments must be balanced for charge.
  • Applying Faraday’s law without correcting for current efficiency; the actual product mass is efficiency × theoretical mass.

Mastering these advanced concepts and their quantitative applications will enable you to solve the most demanding electrochemistry problems in competitive examinations.

hand/cryptography.html:
Authenticated Encryption and AEAD Modes

Authenticated encryption (AE) simultaneously provides confidentiality and integrity. The modern standard is Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD), where a ciphertext is accompanied by a tag that authenticates both the encrypted payload and any unencrypted associated data (AAD). The most widely deployed AEAD constructions are AES‑GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) and ChaCha20‑Poly1305. AES‑GCM combines AES in counter mode with a polynomial‑based MAC over GF(2¹²⁸); it requires a unique 96‑bit nonce per key and produces a 128‑bit tag. ChaCha20‑Poly1305 uses the ChaCha20 stream cipher and the Poly1305 one‑time authenticator, offering comparable performance on platforms lacking AES‑NI. Both schemes are specified in RFC 5116 and RFC 8439 respectively and are mandatory in TLS 1.3.

Other AEAD modes include OCB (Offset Codebook) which achieves optimal block‑cipher calls but is encumbered by patents, and CCM (Counter with CBC‑MAC) used in IEEE 802.11i (WPA2) and constrained environments. CCM requires two passes over the data and a fixed tag length, making it slower than GCM on high‑throughput links. The security of AEAD rests on the underlying primitive’s PRF/PRP security and the uniqueness of nonces; nonce reuse in GCM or ChaCha20‑Poly1305 leads to catastrophic key‑recovery attacks (the “forbidden‑nonce” problem). Implementations therefore enforce deterministic nonce construction (e.g., a 64‑bit counter plus a 32‑bit fixed field) or use synthetic IVs such as AES‑GCM‑SIV (RFC 8452) which tolerates nonce misuse by deriving a per‑message IV from the plaintext.

Associated data is essential for binding protocol metadata (record headers, sequence numbers, algorithm identifiers) to the ciphertext without encrypting it. In TLS 1.3 the record header and the content type are authenticated as AAD, preventing downgrade and truncation attacks. The AEAD interface typically exposes encrypt(key, nonce, plaintext, aad) → (ciphertext, tag) and decrypt(key, nonce, ciphertext, tag, aad) → plaintext or error. Formal models (e.g., the Bellare‑Rogaway AEAD definition) require indistinguishability under chosen‑ciphertext attack (IND‑CCA) and integrity of ciphertexts (INT‑CTXT). Modern libraries (libsodium, OpenSSL, BoringSSL) expose a single‑call API to avoid misuse.

Key Derivation Functions and Password Hashing

Key derivation functions (KDFs) transform high‑entropy secrets or low‑entropy passwords into uniformly distributed cryptographic keys. For high‑entropy inputs (e.g., Diffie‑Hellman shared secrets) a fast extract‑then‑expand KDF such as HKDF (RFC 5869) is used: HKDF‑Extract(salt, IKM) → PRK, then HKDF‑Expand(PRK, info, L) → OKM. HKDF is built on HMAC‑SHA‑256/384/512 and provides provable security in the random‑oracle model. It is employed in TLS 1.3, Signal, and IKEv2 to derive traffic keys from the master secret.

For passwords, memory‑hard KDFs are mandatory to raise the cost of offline brute‑force and GPU/ASIC attacks. PBKDF2 (RFC 2898) iterates HMAC a configurable number of times (typically ≥ 100 000) but is only CPU‑hard; it offers limited resistance to parallel hardware. bcrypt (1999) incorporates a Blowfish‑based key schedule with a configurable cost factor (log₂ rounds) and a 128‑bit salt, providing modest memory hardness. scrypt (2009) introduced a sequential memory‑hard function parameterised by N (CPU/memory cost), r (block size), and p (parallelisation); typical parameters N=2¹⁴, r=8, p=1 require ≈ 16 MiB of RAM per instance. Argon2 (2015, winner of the Password Hashing Competition) comes in three variants: Argon2d (data‑dependent, maximises GPU resistance), Argon2i (data‑independent, side‑channel resistant), and Argon2id (hybrid, recommended for general use). Argon2id with t=3 passes, m=64 MiB, p=4 is a common baseline for web services.

Salt generation must use a CSPRNG; a 128‑bit salt is standard. The output length should match the target algorithm’s key size (e.g., 256 bits for AES‑256). Storing the KDF identifier, parameters, salt, and derived key (or verifier) in a single encoded string (e.g., PHC format) enables future upgrades without breaking existing hashes. Migration strategies include re‑hashing on successful login (lazy upgrade) or a one‑time batch re‑hash with a higher cost factor.

Worked Example: Verifying an Argon2id Hash
A server stores the following PHC string for a user: argon2idv=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$c2FsdHNhbHQ$R2VuZXJhdGVkSGFzaA==. The client sends the password "CorrectHorseBatteryStaple". Show the steps the server takes to verify the password.
1. Parse the PHC string: algorithm=argon2id, version=19, memory=65536 KiB (64 MiB), iterations=3, parallelism=4, salt=base64‑decoded "saltsalt" (8 bytes), hash=base64‑decoded "GeneratedHash" (32 bytes). 2. Using the same parameters, compute Argon2id(password="CorrectHorseBatteryStaple", salt, t=3, m=65536, p=4, hashlen=32). 3. Compare the computed hash with the stored hash using a constant‑time equality function. 4. If they match, authentication succeeds; otherwise reject. The server must not log the password or the derived hash.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “recommended KDF for password storage”, answer Argon2id with concrete parameters (memory ≥ 64 MiB, iterations ≥ 3, parallelism ≥ 1). Mention that PBKDF2 and bcrypt are legacy but still acceptable if Argon2 is unavailable. Cite the PHC string format as the standard storage representation.

Side‑Channel Countermeasures and Implementation Security

Side‑channel attacks exploit physical leakage (timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emanations, cache behaviour) rather than mathematical weaknesses. Constant‑time programming is the primary defence: all secret‑dependent branches and memory accesses must be eliminated. For example, AES‑NI instructions are data‑independent, but a software AES implementation using lookup tables (T‑tables) leaks via cache timing; the fix is to use bitsliced or vectorised constant‑time code. RSA and ECC scalar multiplication must use fixed‑window or Montgomery ladder algorithms with uniform execution flow. Blinding techniques randomise intermediate values: RSA blinding multiplies the ciphertext by rᵉ mod n before exponentiation and removes the factor after; ECC scalar blinding adds a random multiple of the group order to the scalar.

Power analysis (SPA/DPA) targets smart‑cards and embedded devices. Countermeasures include masking (splitting secrets into random shares), hiding (adding noise or dummy operations), and dual‑rail precharge logic at the hardware level. Higher‑order masking (e.g., threshold implementations) protects against combined leakage points. Fault attacks induce errors (voltage glitch, clock glitch, laser) to reveal secret material; detection uses redundancy (duplicate computation, checksums) and infective computation (propagating faults to produce random output). The EMVCo and Common Criteria (ISO 15408) evaluation methodologies define assurance levels (EAL 4+ for payment chips) that mandate side‑channel resistance.

Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre, Meltdown, and PortSmash exploit speculative execution and shared CPU resources. Mitigations include retpoline, kernel page‑table isolation (KPTI), and disabling hyper‑threading for sensitive workloads. Cryptographic libraries (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, libsodium) provide constant‑time APIs and undergo formal verification (e.g., Fiat‑Crypto for field arithmetic, Jasmin for assembly). Developers should prefer high‑level APIs (EVP_AEAD, crypto_aead) over raw primitives and enable compiler hardening flags (-fstack-protector-strong, -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2).

Threshold Cryptography and Distributed Key Generation

Threshold cryptography splits a secret key among n parties such that any t + 1 parties can reconstruct or use the key, while any t or fewer learn nothing. Shamir’s secret sharing (1979) over a finite field 𝔽ₚ underlies most schemes: the dealer picks a random polynomial f(x) of degree t with f(0)=secret, and distributes shares (i, f(i)). Reconstruction uses Lagrange interpolation at x=0. Verifiable secret sharing (VSS) adds commitments (Feldman: gf(i); Pedersen: gf(i)hr(i)) so parties can verify consistency without revealing the secret.

Distributed key generation (DKG) removes the trusted dealer. The classic Pedersen DKG (1991) lets each participant act as a dealer for a Shamir sharing of their own random value; the final secret is the sum of all dealers’ secrets. The protocol tolerates up to t < n/3 malicious parties in the synchronous model. Modern DKGs (e.g., Gennaro‑Jarecki‑Krawczyk‑Rabin 1999, Kate‑Zaverucha‑Goldberg 2010) achieve t < n/2 under a broadcast channel and a common reference string. The resulting public key is the aggregate of individual public keys (e.g., for BLS signatures: pk = Σ pk_i). Threshold signatures (t‑of‑n BLS, t‑of‑n ECDSA via Gennaro‑Goldfeder 2018) enable a group to produce a single valid signature without any party learning the full private key.

Applications include cryptocurrency custody (multi‑sig wallets, threshold ECDSA in Fireblocks, Coinbase), Byzantine fault‑tolerant consensus (Tendermint, HotStuff use threshold BLS for aggregated votes), and secure multiparty computation (MPC) preprocessing. The security proof typically reduces to the hardness of the underlying discrete‑log or pairing problem plus the secrecy of Shamir shares. Implementation pitfalls: side‑channel leakage during share computation, replay attacks on DKG transcripts, and the need for a reliable broadcast channel (often instantiated via a PKI or a blockchain).

Homomorphic Encryption and Secure Computation

Homomorphic encryption (HE) permits computation on ciphertexts, producing an encryption of the result without ever decrypting. The first fully homomorphic scheme (Gentry 2009) used ideal lattices and bootstrapping to refresh noise. Subsequent generations improved efficiency: BGV/BFV (Brakerski‑Gentry‑Vaikuntanathan, Fan‑Vercauteren) support integer arithmetic with modulus switching; CKKS (Cheon‑Kim‑Kim‑Song) enables approximate real‑number arithmetic with rescaling; TFHE (Chillotti‑Gama‑Georgieva‑Izabachène) offers fast Boolean gate evaluation via programmable bootstrapping. All rely on the Learning With Errors (LWE) or Ring‑LWE assumption.

Performance characteristics: BFV/BGV ciphertext size ≈ 2 KB per 128‑bit slot, multiplication depth limited by noise budget (typically 5‑10 levels without bootstrapping). CKKS ciphertexts are similar but support batching (SIMD) of up to 2¹⁵ slots, making it suitable for machine‑learning inference. TFHE bootstraps in ≈ 10 ms per gate on a modern CPU, enabling arbitrary depth but with larger ciphertexts (≈ 1 MB). Libraries: Microsoft SEAL (BFV/CKKS), PALISADE (BFV/BGV/CKKS/TFHE), OpenFHE (unified API), Concrete (TFHE‑based).

Secure computation frameworks combine HE with other primitives. In the client‑server model, the client encrypts inputs, the server evaluates a circuit, and returns the ciphertext. For multi‑party settings, threshold HE (e.g., threshold BFV) distributes the secret key so that decryption requires t + 1 parties. Hybrid protocols (e.g., SPDZ‑style MPC with HE for preprocessing) achieve high throughput for linear layers and use garbled circuits for non‑linear activations. Real‑world deployments: private contact‑tracing (DP‑3T uses additive homomorphic encryption), encrypted database queries (Cipherbase), and privacy‑preserving ML (Google’s Private Join and Compute). The main open challenges are ciphertext size, latency of bootstrapping, and the lack of standardised parameter sets for interoperability.

  • Confusing AEAD nonce requirements: assuming a random nonce is safe for GCM; the standard mandates a unique nonce per key, and reuse leads to key recovery.
  • Treating PBKDF2 as memory‑hard; it is only CPU‑hard and offers limited GPU resistance compared to Argon2 or scrypt.
  • Believing constant‑time code alone defeats all side channels; microarchitectural effects (speculative execution, cache‑line sharing) require additional mitigations.
  • Assuming Shamir secret sharing provides verifiability without commitments; Feldman or Pedersen VSS is needed for malicious‑dealer resistance.
  • Thinking any HE scheme can evaluate arbitrary depth without bootstrapping; leveled schemes have a fixed multiplicative depth determined by noise growth.
  • Overlooking that threshold signatures require a reliable broadcast channel; without it, a malicious party can cause abort or equivocation.
  • Mixing up the security models of IND‑CPA, IND‑CCA, and AEAD (IND‑CCA + INT‑CTXT); exam questions often test the exact definition required for a protocol.
The advanced sections above cover authenticated encryption, key derivation, side‑channel defences, threshold cryptography, and homomorphic encryption with concrete parameters and exam‑focused traps.

hand/surface-chemistry.html:
BET and Multilayer Adsorption Isotherms

The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) model extends the Langmuir monolayer concept to multilayer adsorption on a uniform surface. It assumes that the first layer adsorbs with a heat of adsorption ΔH₁, while subsequent layers adsorb with a heat equal to the latent heat of condensation ΔHₗ. The resulting equation relates the volume of gas adsorbed V at relative pressure P/P₀ to the monolayer capacity Vₘ and the BET constant C:

V = Vₘ × (C × P/P₀) / [(1 − P/P₀) × (1 − P/P₀ + C × P/P₀)]

The BET constant C = exp[(ΔH₁ − ΔHₗ)/RT] reflects the strength of adsorbate–surface interaction relative to adsorbate–adsorbate interaction. A linear BET plot of (P/P₀)/[V(1−P/P₀)] versus P/P₀ yields slope = (C−1)/(VₘC) and intercept = 1/(VₘC). The method is valid typically in the relative pressure range 0.05–0.35; outside this range capillary condensation or monolayer completion distort the linearity. The BET surface area S = Vₘ × Nₐ × σ / 22400 (at STP), where σ is the cross‑sectional area of the adsorbate molecule (e.g., 0.162 nm² for N₂ at 77 K). The model underpins standard surface‑area determination (ISO 9277) and is essential for catalyst support characterisation.

Beyond BET, the Temkin isotherm accounts for a linear decrease in adsorption heat with coverage: θ = (RT/α) ln(K₀P), where α is the heat‑decrease parameter. The Dubinin–Radushkevich (DR) equation, based on pore‑filling theory, expresses adsorption in micropores as ln V = ln V₀ − (A/E)², with A = RT ln(P₀/P) the adsorption potential and E the characteristic energy. The DR model is widely used for activated carbons and zeolites. The Freundlich isotherm (V = K P¹/ⁿ) remains empirical but useful for heterogeneous surfaces where n > 1 indicates favourable adsorption. Each model has a domain of applicability: BET for mesoporous materials, DR for microporous carbons, Temkin for chemisorption on metals, and Freundlich for rough or composite surfaces. Understanding the assumptions behind each isotherm prevents mis‑assignment of surface area or pore‑size distribution in competitive examinations.

Kinetic Models of Heterogeneous Catalysis

Three classical mechanistic frameworks describe the sequence of elementary steps on a solid catalyst surface: Langmuir–Hinshelwood (LH), Eley–Rideal (ER), and Mars–van Krevelen (MvK). In the LH mechanism both reactants adsorb onto adjacent active sites before reacting; the rate law derives from the surface coverages θ_A and θ_B given by Langmuir isotherms. For a bimolecular reaction A + B → products, the rate r = k θ_A θ_B = k K_A K_B P_A P_B / (1 + K_A P_A + K_B P_B)². When one reactant is in large excess, the denominator simplifies and the reaction appears first order in the limiting reactant. The ER mechanism involves one adsorbed species reacting directly with a gas‑phase molecule: r = k θ_A P_B = k K_A P_A P_B / (1 + K_A P_A). This pathway is common for oxidation reactions where O₂ dissociates on the surface and reacts with adsorbed CO or hydrocarbons.

The MvK mechanism is distinctive for redox catalysts (e.g., V₂O₅ in SO₂ oxidation, MoO₃ in selective oxidation). The catalyst lattice oxygen participates in the reaction, creating an oxygen vacancy that is subsequently replenished by gas‑phase O₂. The rate expression often shows a fractional order in O₂ (½–1) and zero order in the hydrocarbon at high coverage. Promoters such as K₂O in Fe for ammonia synthesis increase the electron density of the active metal, lowering the activation barrier for N₂ dissociation. Poisons (S, CO, H₂O) block active sites or alter the electronic structure; for example, sulfur binds strongly to Fe and Ni, suppressing hydrogenation activity. Shape‑selective zeolites (ZSM‑5, β‑zeolite) impose steric constraints: only molecules smaller than the pore aperture (≈0.55 nm for ZSM‑5) access internal acid sites, enabling selective cracking and isomerisation. The turnover frequency (TOF) = rate per active site per second provides a size‑independent activity metric; typical industrial TOFs range from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (ammonia synthesis) to 10² s⁻¹ (fluid catalytic cracking). Kinetic modelling combines these elementary steps with mass‑transfer corrections (Thiele modulus, effectiveness factor) to predict reactor performance.

Worked Example: Distinguishing LH and ER Kinetics
A catalytic oxidation of CO on Pt shows rate r = k P_CO P_O₂ / (1 + K_CO P_CO)² at low CO pressure, but at high CO pressure the rate becomes inversely proportional to P_CO. Identify the operative mechanism and explain the pressure dependence.
At low CO pressure the denominator ≈ 1, giving r ∝ P_CO P_O₂, consistent with both LH and ER. At high CO pressure the term K_CO P_CO dominates the denominator, so r ∝ P_O₂ / P_CO. This inverse CO dependence arises because CO saturates the surface (θ_CO → 1), blocking O₂ adsorption — a hallmark of the Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism where both reactants require vacant sites. In an Eley–Rideal pathway O₂ would react from the gas phase with adsorbed CO, giving r ∝ θ_CO P_O₂ ≈ P_O₂ (zero order in CO). Therefore the observed inverse CO order confirms LH kinetics.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a rate law shows a denominator squared, suspect a bimolecular LH step. If the denominator is linear in one reactant’s pressure, consider ER. Always check limiting‑pressure behaviour: zero order in a reactant often means that reactant’s adsorption is saturated, while negative order signals site blocking. Write the Langmuir coverage expressions first; the algebra then reveals the mechanism without memorising every rate form.

DLVO Theory and Colloidal Stability

The Derjaguin–Landau–Verwey–Overbeek (DLVO) theory quantifies the balance between van der Waals attraction and electrical double‑layer repulsion that governs the stability of lyophobic colloids. The total interaction energy V_T(h) between two identical spherical particles of radius a at surface‑to‑surface separation h is V_T = V_A + V_R. The attractive van der Waals term for spheres (Hamaker approach) is V_A = −A a / (12 h) for h ≪ a, where A is the Hamaker constant (typically 10⁻²⁰–10⁻¹⁹ J for aqueous oxides). The repulsive double‑layer term, derived from the linearised Poisson–Boltzmann equation, is V_R = 2π ε ε₀ a ψ₀² ln[1 + exp(−κh)], where ψ₀ is the surface potential, κ⁻¹ the Debye length, ε the dielectric constant, and ε₀ the vacuum permittivity. The Debye length κ⁻¹ = (ε ε₀ RT / 2F²I)¹/² decreases with ionic strength I; for a 1:1 electrolyte at 25 °C, κ⁻¹ ≈ 0.304/√I (nm, I in mol L⁻¹).

A primary maximum in V_T creates an energy barrier that prevents aggregation; its height depends on ψ₀ and κ⁻¹. When the barrier falls below ~15 kT, rapid coagulation occurs (perikinetic regime). The critical coagulation concentration (CCC) follows the Schulze–Hardy rule: CCC ∝ z⁻⁶ for indifferent electrolytes, where z is the counter‑ion valence. For example, CCC for As₂S₃ sol is ~50 mmol L⁻¹ for Na⁺, ~0.7 mmol L⁻¹ for Ca²⁺, and ~0.01 mmol L⁻¹ for Al³⁺. Specific adsorption of ions can shift the surface potential and alter the CCC dramatically. Steric stabilization, not captured by classical DLVO, arises from adsorbed polymer layers that generate an osmotic repulsion and a volume‑restriction term; the combined theory (extended DLVO) adds a steric potential V_S that decays exponentially with layer thickness. In practice, colloid stability is tuned by pH (which changes ψ₀ via surface protonation), ionic strength, and polymer additives. The zeta potential ζ, measured by electrophoresis, approximates ψ₀ and serves as a practical stability indicator: |ζ| > 30 mV generally ensures kinetic stability.

Phase Inversion and Rheology of Emulsions

Emulsion type (oil‑in‑water O/W or water‑in‑oil W/O) is dictated by the relative affinity of the emulsifier for the two phases, quantified by the hydrophilic‑lipophilic balance (HLB) scale (0–20). Surfactants with HLB > 10 favour O/W emulsions; those with HLB < 10 favour W/O. Bancroft’s rule states that the phase in which the emulsifier is more soluble becomes the continuous phase. Phase inversion can be induced by temperature (phase inversion temperature, PIT), composition (changing oil‑to‑water ratio), or electrolyte addition. For non‑ionic surfactants (e.g., C₁₂E₈), the PIT is the temperature at which the surfactant’s HLB equals the required HLB of the system; near the PIT the interfacial tension reaches a minimum and the emulsion becomes highly unstable, often forming a bicontinuous microemulsion. The PIT correlates with the cloud point of the surfactant and can be predicted from the surfactant’s ethylene oxide number.

Rheological behaviour of concentrated emulsions deviates from Newtonian flow. The effective viscosity η_eff follows the Krieger–Dougherty equation: η_eff = η_c (1 − φ/φ_m)^(−[η]φ_m), where η_c is the continuous‑phase viscosity, φ the dispersed‑phase volume fraction, φ_m the maximum packing fraction (~0.63 for random close packing of spheres), and [η] the intrinsic viscosity (2.5 for hard spheres). At φ > 0.5, emulsions exhibit shear‑thinning due to droplet deformation and alignment; at very high φ they can jam, showing a yield stress described by the Herschel–Bulkley model τ = τ_y + K γ̇ⁿ. Emulsifiers that form rigid interfacial films (e.g., proteins, solid particles — Pickering emulsions) increase the yield stress and impart solid‑like behaviour. Demulsification techniques exploit these rheological signatures: heating above the PIT reduces interfacial tension and promotes coalescence; centrifugation applies a gravitational field that overcomes the energy barrier; adding electrolytes compresses the double layer, lowering the repulsive barrier predicted by DLVO. Understanding the interplay of HLB, PIT, and rheology enables formulation of stable food emulsions (mayonnaise, salad dressings), pharmaceutical creams, and enhanced oil recovery fluids.

Surface Chemistry in Environmental Remediation

Adsorption, catalysis, and colloidal processes are central to modern water and air purification technologies. Activated carbon, with a BET surface area of 800–1500 m² g⁻¹ and a micropore volume of 0.4–0.6 cm³ g⁻¹, removes organic micropollutants (pesticides, pharmaceuticals) via hydrophobic partitioning and π‑π stacking. The adsorption capacity follows the Freundlich isotherm q = K_F C_e¹/ⁿ, where n > 1 indicates favourable uptake. For heavy metals (Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Hg²⁺), surface complexation on oxide minerals (Fe₃O₄, MnO₂) and functionalised biochars is described by the surface complexation model (SCM) with intrinsic stability constants log K_int. Competitive adsorption in multi‑component systems is predicted by the extended Langmuir or ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST).

Photocatalysis using TiO₂ (anatase, band gap 3.2 eV) generates electron‑hole pairs under UV illumination; holes oxidise adsorbed organics or water to •OH radicals, while electrons reduce O₂ to •O₂⁻. The Langmuir–Hinshelwood kinetic model applies: rate = k K C / (1 + K C). Doping with N, C, or transition metals narrows the band gap, extending activity into visible light. Heterogeneous Fenton‑like catalysts (Fe₃O₄, Fe‑zeolites) activate H₂O₂ at neutral pH, producing •OH without the sludge associated with homogeneous Fenton. In air purification, catalytic oxidation of VOCs over MnOₓ‑CeO₂ or Pt/Al₂O₃ follows Mars–van Krevelen redox cycles; the catalyst’s oxygen storage capacity (OSC) determines low‑temperature activity.

Colloidal science underpins membrane filtration and coagulation‑flocculation. Ultrafiltration membranes (pore size 1–100 nm) separate colloidal particles and macromolecules; fouling is mitigated by surface grafting of hydrophilic polymers (PEG, zwitterions) that create a steric barrier. In coagulation, alum (Al₂(SO₄)₃) hydrolyses to Al₁₃O₄(OH)₂₄⁷⁺ (the Al₁₃ polycation) which neutralises negative colloids via charge neutralisation and sweep flocculation. The optimum pH for alum coagulation is 6–7; at higher pH Al(OH)₃ precipitates, reducing efficiency. Polyelectrolyte flocculants (anionic polyacrylamide) bridge particles, forming large flocs that settle rapidly. The zeta potential of the treated water approaches zero at the point of zero charge, signalling effective destabilisation. These principles are integrated in advanced treatment trains: coagulation → flocculation → sedimentation → filtration → adsorption → disinfection, achieving removal of turbidity, pathogens, and trace contaminants to meet stringent regulatory standards.

  • Assuming BET linearity extends beyond the 0.05–0.35 P/P₀ range, leading to overestimated surface areas.
  • Confusing the Eley–Rideal rate law (first order in gas‑phase reactant) with Langmuir–Hinshelwood (second order in surface coverages) when both reactants adsorb.
  • Neglecting the ionic‑strength dependence of the Debye length when applying DLVO, causing erroneous CCC predictions.
  • Treating HLB as an absolute predictor of emulsion type without considering temperature‑induced PIT shifts for non‑ionic surfactants.
  • Overlooking competitive adsorption in multi‑pollutant systems and applying single‑component isotherms directly.
  • Misidentifying the Al₁₃ polycation as the sole active species in alum coagulation while ignoring sweep flocculation at higher doses.
