gat/indian-polity.html:
Anti-Defection Law: Tenth Schedule and Judicial Interpretation

The Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985, seeks to curb political defections by disqualifying legislators who voluntarily give up membership of their party or vote contrary to party directions. The Schedule applies to both Houses of Parliament and State Legislatures. A member incurs disqualification if he or she (a) voluntarily resigns from the party, (b) votes or abstains from voting in the House contrary to any direction issued by the party, or (c) joins another party after election. The Speaker or Chairman of the House decides on disqualification petitions, and the decision is subject to judicial review.

Key judicial pronouncements have shaped the scope of the law. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule but held that the Speaker’s decision is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fide, perversity, or violation of natural justice. The Court also clarified that “voluntarily giving up membership” is not limited to formal resignation; conduct indicating abandonment of party allegiance suffices. In Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India (1994), the Court ruled that a member who publicly opposes the party’s official candidate in an election can be deemed to have voluntarily given up membership. The 91st Amendment Act, 2003, removed the provision allowing a split of one‑third of the legislature party to escape disqualification, thereby tightening the law.

Procedurally, the Speaker must decide within a reasonable time; undue delay has been struck down as a violation of Article 21. The Supreme Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly (2020) directed that disqualification petitions be decided within three months unless exceptional circumstances exist. The law does not apply to mergers where two‑thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge with another party, provided the merger is recognised by the Election Commission. However, the merger exception has been narrowly interpreted to prevent misuse.

Critics argue that the law strengthens party leadership at the expense of individual conscience and intra‑party democracy. The anti‑defection provisions have also been used to engineer defections by encouraging mass resignations, prompting calls for reform such as transferring adjudication to an independent tribunal. The Election Commission has recommended that the power to decide disqualification be vested in the President or Governor on the advice of the Election Commission, a proposal yet to be enacted.

Ordinance Making Power: Constitutional Limits and Judicial Review

Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session, provided the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary. An ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament but must be laid before both Houses when they reassemble. It ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from reassembly unless approved by both Houses earlier. The President may also withdraw an ordinance at any time.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly examined the scope of “satisfaction” and “immediate action”. In R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970), the Court held that the President’s satisfaction is justiciable to the extent of determining whether the requisite circumstances existed; however, the Court refrained from substituting its own judgment for that of the executive. In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Court struck down a series of re‑promulgated ordinances as a “fraud on the Constitution”, establishing that repeated re‑promulgation without legislative approval violates the constitutional scheme. The Court emphasized that ordinance making is an emergency power, not a parallel legislative route.

Further, in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), a seven‑judge bench ruled that an ordinance cannot be used to amend the Constitution, and that the President’s satisfaction must be based on objective material, not merely political expediency. The judgment also clarified that an ordinance lapses if not approved within the stipulated period, and any actions taken under a lapsed ordinance remain valid only if they are not contrary to law. The Court also held that the President cannot promulgate an ordinance on matters that are exclusively within the State List unless the State Legislature is dissolved and the matter is of national importance.

State Governors possess a parallel power under Article 213, subject to the same constraints. The Governor’s ordinance must be reserved for the President’s consideration if it contains provisions that would require Presidential assent if enacted as a State law. The Supreme Court in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) affirmed that the Governor’s satisfaction is also subject to judicial review. The 44th Amendment Act, 1978, inserted a provision that an ordinance cannot be promulgated when the Legislature is in session, reinforcing the principle that ordinance making is exceptional.

Technique: Identifying Constitutional Limits on Ordinance Power
A State Governor promulgates an ordinance on a subject in the State List while the State Legislative Assembly is in session. The ordinance is later challenged in the High Court. What is the most appropriate ground for striking it down?
The ordinance is invalid because Article 213 (mirroring Article 123) permits ordinance making only when the Legislature is not in session. The 44th Amendment explicitly bars promulgation during a session. Therefore, the correct ground is that the Governor lacked constitutional authority to issue the ordinance while the Assembly was sitting, rendering it ultra vires.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the validity of an ordinance, first check whether the Legislature was in session. If it was, the ordinance is automatically void. Next, verify whether the subject falls within the legislative competence of the issuing authority. Finally, recall the D.C. Wadhwa principle: repeated re‑promulgation without legislative approval is a fraud on the Constitution. These three checkpoints cover the majority of ordinance‑related MCQs.

Judicial Appointments: Collegium System, NJAC Judgment and Current Procedure

The appointment of judges to the Supreme Court and High Courts has evolved from executive dominance to a judicially driven collegium system. Under the original constitutional scheme (Articles 124 and 217), the President appoints judges after consultation with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and, for High Courts, the Governor and Chief Justice of the concerned High Court. In S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court held that “consultation” does not mean “concurrence”, giving the executive primacy.

This position was reversed in the Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993) (the Second Judges Case), where a nine‑judge bench ruled that the CJI’s opinion must have primacy and that consultation requires concurrence of the senior most judges. The Court laid down the collegium comprising the CJI and the two senior most Supreme Court judges for Supreme Court appointments, and the CJI plus two senior most judges of the respective High Court for High Court appointments. The Third Judges Case (1998) expanded the Supreme Court collegium to the CJI and four senior most judges, and mandated written reasons for recommendations.

The National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) was introduced by the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014, and the NJAC Act, 2014, to replace the collegium with a six‑member body including the CJI, two senior Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons. In Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) (the Fourth Judges Case), a five‑judge bench struck down the NJAC as unconstitutional, holding that it violated the basic structure by compromising judicial independence and the primacy of the judiciary in appointments. The Court revived the collegium system but directed the government to finalise a Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) in consultation with the CJI to introduce transparency, eligibility criteria, and a complaint mechanism.

As of the latest MoP (2017, revised 2021), the collegium recommends names after evaluating seniority, merit, integrity, and diversity. The government may seek reconsideration once; if the collegium reiterates the recommendation, the appointment must be made. The process for High Court appointments involves the High Court collegium, the State Government, the Supreme Court collegium, and the Union Government. Delays in clearance have been a persistent issue, prompting the Supreme Court in PL v. Union of India (2023) to set timelines for each stage and to warn that inordinate delay may attract contempt proceedings.

Electoral Reforms: NOTA, VVPAT, Election Funding and Disclosure

The introduction of the “None of the Above” (NOTA) option on Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) followed the Supreme Court’s direction in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2013). NOTA allows voters to reject all candidates without violating ballot secrecy. However, NOTA votes are not counted for determining the winner; the candidate with the highest valid votes still wins. The Court clarified that NOTA is a negative vote, not a right to reject, and does not trigger a fresh election even if NOTA votes exceed the winning margin.

Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) was mandated by the Supreme Court in Subramanian Swamy v. Election Commission of India (2013) to enhance transparency. The Court directed that VVPAT be used in all polling stations in a phased manner, with 100% coverage achieved by the 2019 general election. The Election Commission now conducts mandatory random verification of VVPAT slips from five polling stations per Assembly constituency (or per Parliamentary constituency segment) to match electronic counts.

On election funding, the Representation of the People Act, 1951, requires candidates to file expenditure accounts within 30 days of result declaration. The 2017 amendment introduced the Electoral Bond Scheme, allowing anonymous donations through bearer bonds purchased from authorised banks. The Supreme Court in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024) struck down the scheme as violative of the right to information under Article 19(1)(a), holding that anonymity in political funding undermines transparency and facilitates quid pro quo. The Court directed the Election Commission to disclose details of contributions received by political parties.

Further reforms include the introduction of the “Model Code of Conduct” enforcement through the cVIGIL mobile application for citizen reporting of violations, and the linking of Aadhaar with voter IDs (voluntary) to eliminate duplicate entries. The Election Commission has also proposed a cap on cash donations (₹2,000) and mandatory digital transactions for contributions above that threshold, pending legislative approval.

Governor’s Discretionary Powers: Constitutional Provisions and Controversies

Article 163(1) states that the Governor shall act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except where the Constitution requires the Governor to act in his discretion. The discretionary domain is narrow and enumerated: (a) appointment of Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority (Article 164), (b) dismissal of a Ministry that has lost majority but refuses to resign (Article 164), (c) reservation of Bills for Presidential consideration (Article 200), (d) recommendation for President’s Rule under Article 356, and (e) certain functions under the Sixth Schedule for tribal areas.

The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) laid down that the Governor’s report recommending President’s Rule must be based on objective material, and the imposition is subject to judicial review. The Court also held that the Governor cannot act as an agent of the Centre to destabilise elected State governments. In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016), the Court ruled that the Governor’s discretion to summon or dissolve the Assembly must be exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except in situations of constitutional breakdown.

Controversies have arisen over the Governor’s role in appointing Chief Ministers in hung assemblies (e.g., Karnataka 2018, Maharashtra 2019). The Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommended that the Governor should invite the single largest party or pre‑poll alliance, and if none, the post‑poll alliance with the largest number, to form the government. The Punchhi Commission (2010) suggested a fixed tenure of five years for Governors and removal only through impeachment, to insulate the office from political pressure.

The Governor’s power to reserve Bills for Presidential assent has been criticised for delays. In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (2023), the Supreme Court observed that indefinite withholding of assent defeats the legislative process and directed that the Governor must decide within a reasonable time, preferably three months. The Court also clarified that the Governor cannot exercise a pocket veto; once a Bill is passed again by the Legislature after reconsideration, the Governor must give assent.

  • Assuming the anti‑defection law applies to all party members equally; the merger exception and split provisions have distinct thresholds.
  • Confusing the President’s ordinance power with the Governor’s; the Governor must reserve certain Bills for Presidential assent, which the President does not.
  • Believing the collegium system is constitutionally mandated; it is a judicial creation, not a textual provision.
  • Thinking NOTA can trigger a re‑election; it only records dissent and does not affect the outcome.
  • Treating the Governor’s discretionary powers as unlimited; they are confined to specific constitutional situations and subject to judicial review.
  • Overlooking the requirement that ordinances must be laid before the Legislature within six weeks of reassembly; failure leads to automatic lapse.
  • Misreading the NJAC judgment as upholding the commission; it was struck down for violating judicial independence.

These advanced topics illustrate how constitutional provisions interact with judicial interpretation and political practice, a pattern that examiners frequently test through scenario‑based questions.

language/grammar-vocab.html:
Complex Sentence Structures and Clause Types

Understanding how clauses combine to form complex sentences is essential for teaching learners to produce varied and precise written language. A clause contains a subject and a finite verb; clauses are classified as independent (main) or dependent (subordinate). Dependent clauses function as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs within the larger sentence. Noun clauses often begin with subordinating conjunctions such as that, whether, if or wh‑words (what, who, where) and can occupy subject, object, or complement positions (What she said surprised everyone). Adjective (relative) clauses modify nouns and are introduced by relative pronouns (who, which, that, whose, whom) or relative adverbs (where, when, why). Restrictive relative clauses limit the meaning of the antecedent and are not set off by commas, whereas non‑restrictive clauses add extra information and are punctuated with commas. Adverbial clauses express time, cause, condition, concession, purpose, or result and are headed by subordinating conjunctions such as when, because, if, although, so that, in order that. Mastery of these clause types enables teachers to design exercises that move learners from simple coordination (and, but, or) to subordination, thereby expanding syntactic repertoire.

Embedding multiple subordinate clauses creates layers of embedding that increase processing load. For example, The teacher who explained the rule that the students had forgotten was patient contains a relative clause (who explained the rule) that itself embeds a noun clause (that the students had forgotten). Recognising centre‑embedding versus right‑branching structures helps teachers anticipate comprehension difficulties. Centre‑embedding (The rat the cat the dog chased ate died) is far harder to parse than right‑branching (The dog chased the cat that ate the rat). Classroom activities such as clause‑identification grids, transformation drills (convert a simple sentence into a complex one by adding a subordinate clause), and sentence‑combining tasks develop both receptive and productive control.

Punctuation rules accompany clause boundaries. A subordinate clause preceding the main clause is usually followed by a comma (Because it rained, the match was cancelled), whereas a following subordinate clause typically does not require a comma (The match was cancelled because it rained). However, non‑restrictive relative clauses always take commas regardless of position. Teachers should highlight these conventions through contrastive examples and guided editing tasks.

Morphological Processes in Word Formation

Morphology, the study of word structure, provides the toolkit for systematic vocabulary expansion. The primary processes are affixation (prefixation and suffixation), compounding, conversion (zero‑derivation), back‑formation, clipping, blending, and borrowing. Prefixes in English are predominantly derivational and rarely change word class (un‑, re‑, pre‑, mis‑, dis‑), while suffixes can be derivational (-ness, -tion, -able, -ize) or inflectional (-s, -ed, -ing, -er, -est). Derivational suffixes often shift part of speech: teach (verb) → teacher (noun) → teachable (adjective). Inflectional suffixes never alter lexical category and follow a fixed order: plural/possessive before tense/aspect markers (cats, walked, walking).

Compounding joins two or more free morphemes to create a new lexical item. Compounds can be endocentric (blackboard – a type of board), exocentric (pickpocket – not a type of pocket), copulative (bittersweet), or appositional (maidservant). Stress patterns often distinguish compounds from phrases: primary stress on the first element in noun‑noun compounds (greenhouse vs. green house). Conversion allows a word to function in a new syntactic category without overt affixation (email (noun) → to email (verb)). Back‑formation removes an apparent affix to create a new base, as in editor → edit or television → televise. Clipping shortens a word without changing meaning (laboratory → lab, mathematics → maths). Blending fuses parts of two words (smog = smoke + fog, brunch = breakfast + lunch). Borrowing imports lexical items from other languages, often retaining original morphology (kindergarten, tsunami, algorithm).

Teaching morphology explicitly helps learners decode unfamiliar words. Root‑word analysis (identifying Latin/Greek bases such as port, spect, dict) combined with affix knowledge enables inference of meaning (portable, inspect, dictate). Word‑family maps, morphological matrices, and affix‑sorting games reinforce pattern recognition. Assessment can include tasks where students segment polymorphemic words, label each morpheme’s function, and generate new forms by adding or substituting affixes.

Clause Transformation Drill
Rewrite the following simple sentence as a complex sentence containing a noun clause, an adjective clause, and an adverbial clause of reason: "The manager approved the proposal."
One possible answer: "Because the data supported the plan, the manager, who reviewed the report carefully, approved the proposal that the team had prepared." Explanation: Because the data supported the plan is an adverbial clause of reason (fronted, followed by a comma). who reviewed the report carefully is a non‑restrictive adjective clause modifying the manager (set off by commas). that the team had prepared is a restrictive noun clause functioning as the direct object of approved (no commas).
Exam‑Day Strategy for Clause Questions
When a question asks you to identify clause types, first locate all finite verbs. Each finite verb signals a clause. Then decide whether the clause can stand alone (independent) or depends on a subordinating conjunction/relative pronoun (dependent). Label the dependent clause by its function: subject/object/complement → noun clause; modifies a noun → adjective clause; modifies the verb/adjective/adverb of the main clause → adverbial clause. This systematic scan prevents mis‑classifying embedded clauses.

Discourse Markers and Cohesive Devices

Beyond sentence‑level grammar, coherent texts rely on discourse markers and cohesive devices that signal relationships between ideas. Discourse markers (also called pragmatic markers) include conjunctions (however, therefore, moreover), adverbials (consequently, meanwhile, in contrast), and lexical phrases (on the other hand, for instance, as a result). They operate at the interpersonal and textual metafunctions, guiding the reader’s interpretation of stance, sequencing, and logical flow. Cohesion, as described by Halliday and Hasan, comprises reference (pronouns, demonstratives, comparatives), substitution (do so, the same), ellipsis (omission of recoverable elements), conjunction (explicit logical connectors), and lexical cohesion (reiteration, synonymy, hyponymy, meronymy, collocation). Effective teaching integrates both dimensions: students learn to use however to signal contrast, furthermore for addition, and in conclusion for closure, while also practicing pronoun chains that maintain referential continuity across paragraphs.

Reference chains illustrate how a participant introduced early (the scientist) can be tracked via pronouns (he, his), demonstratives (this researcher), or lexical repetition (the expert). Breaks in the chain cause ambiguity. Substitution and ellipsis reduce redundancy: She likes apples, and he does too (substitution) versus She likes apples, and he likes ___ too (ellipsis). Conjunction types mirror logical relations: additive (and, also), adversative (but, yet), causal (so, because), temporal (then, afterwards). Lexical cohesion is reinforced through thematic vocabulary clusters; a paragraph on climate change will repeatedly deploy emissions, temperature, mitigation, adaptation and their synonyms.

Classroom tasks include marker‑insertion exercises (provide a text with blanks for appropriate discourse markers), cohesion‑analysis worksheets (highlight reference chains, substitution, ellipsis), and paragraph‑reordering activities where students justify ordering using cohesive cues. Assessment rubrics should reward appropriate marker variety, accurate reference tracking, and logical conjunction use rather than mere presence of connectors.

Error Analysis and Remedial Teaching Strategies

Systematic error analysis moves beyond surface correction to uncover the cognitive and linguistic sources of learner mistakes. Errors are classified as interlingual (transfer from L1), intralingual (overgeneralisation, incomplete rule application), developmental (stage‑appropriate hypotheses), and induced (instructional gaps). For example, a Hindi‑speaking learner may produce He is going to school yesterday (interlingual tense transfer), while a learner who says She goed exhibits overgeneralisation of the regular past‑tense rule (intralingual). Developmental errors such as Why you are late? reflect a transitional question‑formation stage. Induced errors arise when teaching materials present rules without sufficient contextualised practice.

Error‑gravity assessment helps prioritise remediation. Global errors impede communication (wrong word order, missing clause connectors) and warrant immediate attention; local errors (article omission, minor preposition choice) may be addressed later. Remedial strategies include contrastive analysis tasks (compare L1 and L2 structures), focused practice on the specific rule (drills, guided writing), metalinguistic explanation (explicit rule statement with examples), and corrective feedback techniques: recasts (implicit reformulation), explicit correction, clarification requests, and elicitation (prompting self‑repair). Research shows that a combination of explicit instruction and meaning‑focused practice yields durable gains.

Diagnostic tools such as error‑tagged corpora, learner‑produced writing samples, and oral recordings enable teachers to map error profiles for individuals or groups. A remedial cycle: (1) collect data, (2) categorise errors, (3) select high‑frequency global errors, (4) design targeted mini‑lessons, (5) provide practice with immediate feedback, (6) reassess after a suitable interval. Documentation of error reduction over time informs both learner progress reports and curriculum adjustment.

  • Confusing restrictive and non‑restrictive relative clauses, leading to comma misuse.
  • Treating all subordinate clauses as adverbial, missing noun‑clause functions.
  • Assuming every affix changes word class; overlooking inflectional suffixes.
  • Overusing a single discourse marker (e.g., however) instead of varying cohesive devices.
  • Applying blanket correction to all errors without distinguishing global from local impact.
  • Neglecting to teach the stress pattern difference between compounds and phrases.
  • Failing to provide metalinguistic explanations after recasts, leaving learners unaware of the rule.
